claims.text: Sintering at 900–980 °C triggers precipitation of a continuous nanoscale network of Ti-rich and V-rich B2/B19 intermetallics at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary intermetallic network suppresses Mg volatilization by acting as a diffusion barrier.
The precipitates accelerate densification through grain-boundary pinning.
The precipitate network maximizes alloy hardness.
Sintering in the proposed range forms a protective Cr/Fe-enriched passive oxide layer.
The ball-milled starting powder is a metastable BCC solid solution.
The ball-milled powder has a high defect density.
The ball-milled powder has high oxygen content.
Keeping the sintering temperature below 1000 °C prevents substantial Mg loss.
Temperatures above 800 °C are required to provide sufficient atomic mobility for phase separation and densification.
A high thermodynamic driving force for phase separation at 900–980 °C causes nucleation of refractory intermetallics.
The refractory precipitates slow outward Mg diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion.
Slower Mg and oxygen diffusion prevents formation of porous, non-protective oxides.
Precipitate pinning inhibits grain growth and preserves a fine-grained microstructure that enhances hardness.
Localized stress fields around the precipitates facilitate pore elimination.
The proposed processing window yields a bulk alloy with greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed processing window yields significantly higher hardness than sintering below 800 °C.
The resulting passive film has a Cr/Fe-enriched outer layer and a dense Mg-depleted inner layer.
Exceeding 1000 °C causes rapid Mg volatilization and disrupts the stoichiometry needed for the intermetallic network.
Excessive dwell time coarsens the precipitates and reduces their diffusion-barrier efficacy.

contradictions.description: The stated alloy contains Mg, Al, Ti, V, Fe, and Co but no Cr, while the hypothesis predicts a Cr/Fe-enriched passive layer without identifying any Cr source.
